rules.title: The primary name server limits concurrent zone transfers to authorized secondary name servers
rules.explanation: The BIND server transfers option limits how many concurrent zone transfers a primary name server may perform with authorized secondary name servers. Zone transfers use TCP and move entire zone datasets between servers.
rules.impact: Unbounded concurrent zone transfers can exhaust network and server resources and enable denial-of-service conditions. Limiting concurrent transfers reduces that risk while still allowing authorized secondaries to obtain zone updates.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement server, substatement transfers

rules.title: The secondary name server limits the number of zones requested from a single primary name server
rules.explanation: The BIND transfers-per-ns option limits how many concurrent zone transfers a secondary name server may request from any single primary name server.
rules.impact: Excessive concurrent transfers from one primary can overload that server and disrupt DNS availability. Capping per-primary transfer concurrency helps preserve capacity for legitimate zone synchronization.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, substatement transfers-per-ns

rules.title: The secondary name server limits the total number of zones requested at one time
rules.explanation: The BIND transfers-in option limits the total number of concurrent inbound zone transfers a secondary name server may request at any one time.
rules.impact: Too many simultaneous inbound transfers can exhaust local resources and degrade DNS service. A global inbound transfer limit reduces denial-of-service exposure from transfer storms.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, substatement transfers-in

rules.title: The name server limits simultaneous client connections for allowed dynamic update clients
rules.explanation: The BIND transfers-out option limits concurrent outbound zone-transfer sessions that a name server may sustain for authorized clients, including those permitted to perform dynamic updates.
rules.impact: Unlimited concurrent TCP sessions used for transfers and updates can exhaust server capacity and cause denial of service. Constraining concurrent outbound transfer sessions reduces that risk.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, substatement transfers-out

rules.title: The print-severity logging option generates audit records that identify event types
rules.explanation: The BIND print-severity logging option includes the severity level of each logged message. Severity helps classify what type of event occurred in the audit trail.
rules.impact: Without severity information, operators cannot readily distinguish informational, warning, and error events during incident analysis. Including severity improves forensic usefulness of DNS logs.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, substatement print-severity

rules.title: The print-time logging option records the date and time of events
rules.explanation: The BIND print-time logging option includes a timestamp on each log message so administrators can establish when events occurred.
rules.impact: Event correlation and forensic investigation depend on reliable timestamps. Without print-time, reconstructing incident timelines from DNS logs is severely limited.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, substatement print-time

rules.title: The print-category logging option records which process category generated events
rules.explanation: The BIND print-category logging option records the logging category associated with each message, indicating which DNS server component or facility produced the event.
rules.impact: Knowing which BIND category generated an event aids triage and root-cause analysis. Without category context, correlating log entries to DNS functions during an incident is more difficult.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, substatement print-category

rules.title: The name server is configured to audit DNS components by selectable criteria and record security-relevant outcomes
rules.explanation: BIND logging channels and categories control which DNS events are audited and where records are written. Proper channel and category configuration enables selectable event criteria and capture of failed security checks, event outcomes, and sources needed for recovery analysis.
rules.impact: Without comprehensive DNS audit records, security teams cannot reliably detect, investigate, or attribute incidents involving the name server. Inadequate logging also hinders returning services to a known operational state after failures.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, channel and category

rules.title: The ZSK private key is the only DNSSEC private key stored on name servers that support dynamic updates
rules.explanation: On a DNSSEC-enabled BIND primary that accepts dynamic updates, the Zone Signing Key (ZSK) private key must remain online so newly updated RRsets can be signed immediately. The Key Signing Key (KSK) private key should not also be stored on that server.
rules.impact: Keeping the KSK private key offline limits the blast radius if the Internet-facing name server is compromised. Exposure of both ZSK and KSK private keys would allow an attacker to forge trusted DNSSEC signatures and undermine zone authenticity.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement allow-update; verify signed zone files and ZSK .private key files

rules.title: KSK signature generation is performed offline with the KSK private key stored offline
rules.explanation: The Key Signing Key (KSK) is used to sign DNSKEY RRsets that establish the DNSSEC trust for a zone. Signature generation with the KSK private key should be performed offline, and that private key should not reside on the online name server.
rules.impact: Compromise of an online KSK private key can allow undetected substitution of zone signing material and redirection of clients to fraudulent destinations. Offline KSK handling protects the top of the zone trust chain.
rules.scope: Settings in signed zone files; presence of KSK .private key files on the server file system

rules.title: The key file used by the name server is owned by the account running the name server software
rules.explanation: TSIG and related key files referenced by BIND contain secret material used to authenticate DNS transactions. File ownership should match the account under which the name server process runs.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership can allow unauthorized users to read or replace shared secrets. Compromised key material defeats message authentication for zone transfers, dynamic updates, and other protected transactions.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: TSIG key file location and permissions

rules.title: Read and write access to the TSIG key file is restricted to the account running the name server software
rules.explanation: The TSIG key file holds shared secrets used by BIND for Transaction Signature authentication. Permissions should allow only the name server account to read and write that file.
rules.impact: Weak permissions may let an attacker recover or alter TSIG secrets. Altered or disclosed keys enable forged or intercepted authenticated DNS messages.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: TSIG key file location and permissions

rules.title: A unique TSIG key is generated for each pair of communicating hosts
rules.explanation: TSIG authenticates DNS messages between hosts that share a secret key, typically encoded in Base64 and configured in named.conf. Each communicating host pair should use its own unique TSIG key.
rules.impact: Reusing one TSIG key across many peers expands the impact of a single key compromise. Unique per-pair keys preserve origin authentication and integrity for zone transfers and other protected transactions.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements key and allow-transfer; verify unique use of TSIG key pairs

rules.title: TSIG keys used by the name server are owned by a privileged account
rules.explanation: TSIG key files store shared secrets used to authenticate BIND server-to-server and update transactions. Those files should be owned by a privileged administrative account.
rules.impact: Non-privileged ownership increases the chance that unauthorized users can modify or replace TSIG material. Compromised ownership undermines authenticated DNS messaging.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: TSIG key file location and owner

rules.title: TSIG keys used by the name server are group-owned by a privileged account
rules.explanation: Group ownership of TSIG key files controls which accounts can access shared authentication secrets through group permissions. The group owner should be a privileged administrative account.
rules.impact: An overly broad or unprivileged group owner can expose TSIG secrets to unnecessary accounts. Restricting group ownership helps preserve confidentiality and integrity of authenticated DNS transactions.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: TSIG key file location and group owner

rules.title: Split-zone resource records for external and internal hosts are maintained in separate datasets
rules.explanation: In a split DNS design, zones that serve both external and internal clients should keep public and private resource records in separate zone datasets or views. External clients should receive only publicly intended RRs.
rules.impact: Mixing internal and external RRs in one dataset can leak private hostnames and addressing to untrusted resolvers. Separation supports least disclosure of internal infrastructure.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements view; verify zone files in use and their contents

rules.title: The internal name server in a split DNS configuration is unreachable by external resolvers
rules.explanation: In split DNS deployments that use separate internal and external name servers, the internal server should accept queries only from internal clients. External resolvers should not be able to reach it.
rules.impact: An internally facing name server that answers external queries can expose private naming data and enlarge the attack surface. Restricting reachability confines internal DNS information to authorized networks.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement view "internal", substatement match-clients

rules.title: The external name server in a split DNS configuration is unreachable by internal resolvers
rules.explanation: In split DNS deployments that use separate internal and external name servers, the external server should serve external clients and not be used by internal resolvers. Internal clients should query internal name servers instead.
rules.impact: Allowing internal resolvers to use the external name server can blur role separation and return incomplete or inconsistent views of internal names. Keeping external DNS unreachable to internal resolvers reinforces split-DNS isolation.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement view "external", substatement match-clients

rules.title: The hidden primary authoritative name server IP address does not appear in the zone NS set
rules.explanation: A hidden primary is an authoritative name server whose address is omitted from the published NS RRset. Visible name servers obtain zone data from the hidden primary via zone transfer while appearing as the zone's public name servers.
rules.impact: Publishing the primary's address concentrates attacker attention on the authoritative source of zone data. Hiding the primary reduces the likelihood of direct targeting of the master zone server.
rules.scope: Settings in zone files; hidden primary name server IP address

rules.title: NSEC3 is used for all internal DNSSEC-signed zones
rules.explanation: NSEC3 is a DNSSEC authenticated-denial-of-existence mechanism that proves a queried name or RR type is absent without enabling trivial zone enumeration the way NSEC can. Internal signed zones should use NSEC3.
rules.impact: NSEC chains can make it easier to walk a zone and discover names that were not intended to be enumerated. NSEC3 reduces that disclosure risk for internal DNS namespaces while still providing authenticated nonexistence.
rules.scope: Settings in signed zone files; presence of NSEC or NSEC3

rules.title: ZSK and KSK private keys are not stored on DNSSEC primary servers that do not support dynamic updates
rules.explanation: When a DNSSEC-enabled primary does not accept dynamic updates, zone signing can be performed offline. In that case, neither the ZSK nor the KSK private key needs to remain on the online authoritative server.
rules.impact: Storing private signing keys on an Internet-facing server unnecessarily exposes them to compromise. Offline key storage protects DNSSEC trust material when online resigning is not required.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement allow-update; verify ZSK/KSK private keys exist on the file system

rules.title: Dnssec-keygen output files are owned by root or deleted after installation into the name server key file
rules.explanation: The dnssec-keygen utility creates key pair files that may later be copied into the operational key material used by BIND. After installation, those generated files should be owned by root or removed.
rules.impact: Lingering key-generation artifacts with weak ownership can expose private key material. Proper ownership or deletion reduces unauthorized access to cryptographic secrets.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: location of dnssec-keygen-generated files and owner

rules.title: Dnssec-keygen output files are group-owned by the name server administrator account or deleted after installation
rules.explanation: Files produced by dnssec-keygen contain sensitive key material before and after they are installed for BIND use. Their group owner should be the DNS administrator account, or the files should be deleted after copying into the operational key file.
rules.impact: Incorrect group ownership can grant unnecessary accounts access to private keys. Restricting or removing these files limits disclosure and tampering risk.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: location of dnssec-keygen-generated files and group owner

rules.title: Dnssec-keygen key file permissions grant read-only access to the owner and deny access to all others
rules.explanation: Key files generated by dnssec-keygen store cryptographic material used to protect DNS transactions and DNSSEC signing. Permissions should allow only the owner to read the files and deny access to all other users.
rules.impact: World-readable or writable key files enable theft or modification of secrets. Strict read-only owner permissions help preserve authentication and integrity guarantees.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: location of dnssec-keygen-generated files and permissions

rules.title: The ZSK private key on servers that accept dynamic updates is owned by root
rules.explanation: On DNSSEC primaries that accept dynamic updates, the ZSK private key must remain online so updated RRsets can be resigned. That private key file should be owned by root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized ownership of an online ZSK private key can allow forged signatures for dynamically updated zone data. Root ownership helps restrict access to this high-value signing secret.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: ZSK private key location and owner

rules.title: The ZSK private key on servers that accept dynamic updates is group-owned by root
rules.explanation: The online ZSK private key used for dynamic update resigning should have root as its group owner so group-based access remains tightly controlled.
rules.impact: A non-root group owner may expand read access to the ZSK private key beyond administrators. Restricting group ownership reduces the chance of signature-key compromise.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: ZSK private key location and group owner

rules.title: Secondary name servers initiate zone update notifications to other authoritative name servers
rules.explanation: DNS NOTIFY messages alert other authoritative servers that zone data has changed so they can refresh and transfer updates promptly. Secondary servers should be configured to send NOTIFY announcements to other authoritative servers for the zone, using notify and also-notify as appropriate.
rules.impact: If secondaries do not propagate NOTIFY messages, some authoritative servers may continue serving stale zone data. Timely notifications help maintain zone consistency across the authoritative set.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements options and zone, substatements notify and also-notify

rules.title: Recursion is disabled on authoritative name servers
rules.explanation: Recursion causes a name server to resolve queries on behalf of clients by chasing referrals and caching answers. Authoritative BIND servers should disable recursion so they answer only for zones they serve.
rules.impact: Recursive authoritative servers are more susceptible to cache poisoning and can be abused as open resolvers. Disabling recursion on authoritative servers reduces poisoning risk and keeps authoritative and resolving roles separated.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, substatements recursion, allow-query, allow-recursion; statement zone, substatement allow-query

rules.title: Primary name servers notify authorized secondary name servers when zone files are updated
rules.explanation: When a primary detects a zone serial number change, it should send NOTIFY messages to authorized secondary name servers. Secondaries can then query the SOA and transfer the updated zone if needed.
rules.impact: Without NOTIFY, secondaries may rely solely on refresh timers and serve outdated data for longer periods. Prompt notification supports zone integrity and consistent authoritative answers.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements options and zone, substatements notify and also-notify

rules.title: All root name servers listed in the local root hints file are valid
rules.explanation: Caching and resolving name servers use a local root hints (or root zone) file as the starting point for iterative resolution. Entries in that file should identify valid root name servers for the DNS root.
rules.impact: Tampered or invalid root hints can redirect resolution through rogue servers and undermine all subsequent name lookups. Valid root hints preserve a trustworthy bootstrap for recursive resolution.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, zone type "hint"; contents of the specified root zone file

rules.title: Root hints on authoritative name servers are empty or removed
rules.explanation: Authoritative-only name servers should not perform recursive resolution and therefore should not rely on a populated root hints file. Root hints should be empty or removed so the server does not refer or recurse via the root.
rules.impact: Root hints on an authoritative server can enable unintended query handling for zones the server does not own. Removing them helps keep the server focused on authoritative answers and reduces caching or referral abuse.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, zone type "hint" and associated file

rules.title: Authoritative name servers accept zone transfer requests only from specified secondary name servers
rules.explanation: The BIND allow-transfer access control list defines which hosts may request AXFR or IXFR zone transfers. Authoritative servers should permit transfers only from designated secondary name servers.
rules.impact: Unrestricted zone transfers can disclose full zone contents and increase denial-of-service load on primaries. Limiting transfers to authorized secondaries protects confidential naming data and server capacity.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement zone, substatement allow-transfer

rules.title: The name server implementation separates internal and external DNS roles
rules.explanation: Internal and external DNS roles determine which clients may query which views or servers and which resource records are visible. BIND views, match-clients ACLs, and network placement are used to enforce that separation.
rules.impact: Failure to separate roles can leak private address space and internal hostnames into public DNS. Role isolation reduces reconnaissance value for attackers probing the private network.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements view, substatement match-clients; view order; network segments

rules.title: Outbound DNS messages are sent from a random ephemeral port
rules.explanation: BIND can be configured to source outbound DNS queries from a fixed port or from ephemeral ports allocated by the operating system. Outbound messages should use a random ephemeral source port rather than a static port setting.
rules.impact: Predictable source ports make it easier for attackers to forge responses to outstanding queries. Random ephemeral ports increase the difficulty of successful spoofing and cache poisoning.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, port flag (except listen-on/listen-on-v6)

rules.title: The host running the name server uses a dedicated management interface
rules.explanation: A dedicated management interface separates administrative traffic from DNS service traffic on the name server host. Management access should use that out-of-band path rather than the DNS-facing interface.
rules.impact: Mixing management and production DNS traffic increases exposure of administrative services to attackers targeting the DNS path. A dedicated management channel improves resilience when the DNS network is degraded or compromised.
rules.scope: Parameters: ifconfig -a command output; presence of a dedicated management interface

rules.title: Primary name server configuration and zone files are group-owned by a DNS administration group
rules.explanation: Core BIND files such as named.conf, root hints, and zone files should be group-owned by a group reserved for DNS administration. That group membership controls shared administrative access through filesystem permissions.
rules.impact: Overly broad group ownership can allow unauthorized modification of authoritative data and server configuration. Restricting group ownership supports least-privilege discretionary access control for DNS content.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: location of core BIND files (named.conf, root hints, zone files) and group owner

rules.title: Name server core files are owned by root or the name server process account
rules.explanation: Core BIND configuration and zone files should be owned by root or by the account under which the named process runs. Ownership determines who can permanently alter authoritative configuration and data.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership can let unauthorized users change zone content or server settings. Proper ownership protects the integrity of DNS configuration and published records.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: location of core BIND files (named.conf, root hints, zone files) and owner

rules.title: Name server software is started with restricted privileges
rules.explanation: BIND should run as an unprivileged dedicated account rather than as root after startup. Restricting process privileges limits filesystem and system access available to the name server daemon.
rules.impact: A compromised name server running as root can lead to full host takeover. Running with reduced privileges contains damage if the DNS process is exploited.
rules.scope: Parameters: ps -ef command output

rules.title: TSIG and DNSSEC keys are not used for more than one year
rules.explanation: TSIG and DNSSEC cryptographic keys protect authentication and integrity of DNS data and transactions. Keys should be rotated so that no key remains in operational use longer than one year.
rules.impact: Long-lived keys increase the window during which a stolen or weakly protected key can be abused. Regular rotation limits exposure and aligns cryptographic material with organizational security baselines.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: DNSSEC and TSIG cryptographic key files and their creation date

rules.title: Permissions on primary name server files follow least privilege
rules.explanation: Filesystem permissions on named.conf, zone files, and related core BIND files should grant only the access required for operation and administration. Excess read or write rights for other users should be removed.
rules.impact: Overly permissive file modes allow unauthorized viewing or modification of DNS configuration and zone data. Least-privilege permissions reduce accidental and malicious change risk.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: location of core BIND files (named.conf, root hints, zone files) and permissions

rules.title: The host running the name server applies a firewall rule set that restricts DNS interface traffic
rules.explanation: Host-based firewall rules on the DNS interface should allow only the ports and protocols required for DNS service, typically 53/tcp and 53/udp. Other inbound traffic on that interface should be denied.
rules.impact: An unrestricted DNS host interface exposes unused services to remote attack and flood traffic. Tight firewall filtering reduces packet-flood and lateral-abuse risk against the name server platform.
rules.scope: Parameters: host-based firewall rules (for example, iptables) for the DNS interface, restricted to ports 53/tcp and 53/udp

rules.title: The name server protects DNS data integrity and authenticity with DNSSEC
rules.explanation: DNSSEC provides data origin authentication and integrity protection for DNS information through digital signatures and a chain of trust, including DNSKEY and Delegation Signer (DS) validation. BIND should enable DNSSEC so signed zone data can be validated end to end.
rules.impact: Without DNSSEC validation, resolvers may accept forged, truncated, or cache-poisoned answers. Broken or missing trust chains allow rogue servers to inject false DNS data that is difficult to detect.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement dnssec-enable; signed zone files, presence of DNSKEY

rules.title: Log records are generated for authentication failures, signed-transfer anomalies, service start and stop, and other name server events
rules.explanation: BIND logging severity and category settings control whether security-relevant DNS events are recorded. The server should generate log records for identity-binding verification errors, anomalies in signed zone transfers, successful and unsuccessful service start and stop, and other name server events.
rules.impact: Incomplete logging leaves gaps in intrusion detection and forensic reconstruction. Capturing authentication failures and transfer anomalies is especially important for detecting DNSSEC or TSIG misuse.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, substatement severity (set to "info")

rules.title: The name server uses only approved ports and protocols
rules.explanation: The BIND listen-on port setting and related listener configuration determine which local ports accept DNS traffic. The implementation should listen only on organization-approved ports and protocols for DNS service.
rules.impact: Unnecessary listeners expand the network attack surface and can enable unauthorized tunneling or service abuse. Restricting ports and protocols supports least functionality on the name server.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, substatement listen-on port

rules.title: The name server uniquely authenticates peers before zone transfers or dynamic updates
rules.explanation: Server-to-server DNS transactions such as zone transfers and dynamic updates should use cryptographically sound mutual authentication, typically via TSIG with per-peer keys configured in named.conf. The server should identify and authenticate the peer before honoring those requests.
rules.impact: Unauthenticated transfers and updates allow impersonation of authorized name servers and injection of false zone data. Mutual authentication protects integrity of DNS information exchanged between servers.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements key, allow-transfer (on the primary), server and keys (on the secondary)

rules.title: Separate TSIG key pairs protect transactions between each pair of servers
rules.explanation: TSIG key pairs used for BIND server-to-server authentication should be unique to each communicating server pair rather than shared broadly. Separate keys isolate trust relationships between peers.
rules.impact: A shared TSIG key across many servers means one compromise can affect all of those relationships. Distinct per-pair keys limit blast radius and simplify recovery after key exposure.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements key; verify unique use of TSIG key pairs

rules.title: The name server runs in a chroot directory structure
rules.explanation: A chroot jail confines the BIND process to a restricted directory tree so it cannot access the rest of the host filesystem. The name server should be started within such a chroot environment.
rules.impact: If the DNS process is exploited, unrestricted filesystem access enables broader host compromise. Chroot containment limits an attacker's ability to reach other files and commands on the system.
rules.scope: Parameters: ps -ef command output

rules.title: Caching name servers restrict recursive queries to known supported clients
rules.explanation: Caching or recursive BIND servers should use allow-query and allow-recursion ACLs so only known client addresses and ranges can request recursion. Unknown or untrusted sources should be denied recursive service.
rules.impact: Open recursion enables cache poisoning attempts and amplifies abuse by third parties. Restricting recursive clients protects resolver integrity and reduces unauthorized use of the caching service.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, substatements allow-query and allow-recursion; ACL definition

rules.title: The name server manages capacity and redundancy to limit denial-of-service impact from query flooding
rules.explanation: DNS implementations can limit exposure to flood-based denial of service through recursion controls, query ACLs, capacity planning, and architectural redundancy. BIND options such as recursion and allow-query contribute to that defensive posture.
rules.impact: DNS outages cascade quickly because clients depend on name resolution for nearly all network services. Capacity, redundancy, and query restrictions reduce the impact of spoofed and amplified flood attacks.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement options, substatements recursion, allow-query; statement zone, substatement allow-query

rules.title: DNSSEC key file permissions grant read-only access to the owner and deny access to all others
rules.explanation: DNSSEC private and related key files stored on disk protect signing material for authenticating zone data. Permissions should allow only the owner to read the keys and deny access to all other users.
rules.impact: Readable or writable DNSSEC keys at rest can be stolen or altered if the host is accessed by unauthorized users. Strict permissions protect confidentiality of signing keys and integrity of signed DNS data.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: DNSSEC key location and permissions

rules.title: DNSSEC keys used by the implementation are owned by a privileged account
rules.explanation: DNSSEC key files on the name server filesystem should be owned by a privileged administrative account. Ownership controls who can replace or manage signing material at rest.
rules.impact: Non-privileged ownership increases the risk that unauthorized users can tamper with DNSSEC keys. Proper ownership helps protect the authenticity of signed zone data.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: DNSSEC key location and owner

rules.title: DNSSEC keys used by the implementation are group-owned by a privileged account
rules.explanation: Group ownership of DNSSEC key files determines which secondary accounts can access signing material through group permissions. The group owner should be a privileged administrative account.
rules.impact: An inappropriate group owner can expose private signing keys to unnecessary users. Restricting group ownership reduces unauthorized disclosure or modification of DNSSEC material.
rules.scope: Settings in the file system: DNSSEC key location and group owner

rules.title: The name server retains at least three versions of the local log file
rules.explanation: BIND logging file channels support a versions parameter that controls how many rotated copies of a local log file are retained. At least three versions should be kept.
rules.impact: Insufficient log retention can erase evidence needed for troubleshooting and incident response. Keeping multiple versions preserves recent DNS transaction history on the local system.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, substatement file, parameter versions (must be >=3)

rules.title: The name server is configured with a channel that writes audit records to a local file
rules.explanation: A BIND logging channel can direct selected categories of DNS events to a local file. The implementation should include such a channel so audit records are stored on the host.
rules.impact: Without local audit files, administrators lack an on-host record of DNS activity for triage and forensics. Local logging provides a baseline evidence source even when remote collectors are unavailable.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, channel, that sends audit to a local file

rules.title: The name server is configured with a channel that sends audit records to a remote syslog
rules.explanation: BIND can send logging output through a syslog channel, which the host syslog or rsyslog service can forward to a remote collector. The implementation should configure remote delivery of audit records.
rules.impact: Logs that exist only on the name server can be lost if the host is compromised or fails. Remote syslog retention preserves audit evidence outside the audited system.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statement logging, channel, that sends audit to syslog; syslog/rsyslog remote-forwarding configuration

rules.title: Mutually authenticated sessions protect zone transfers and other server-to-server DNS transactions
rules.explanation: Zone transfers and related server-to-server DNS transactions should use cryptographically sound mutual authentication, such as TSIG, so each peer verifies the other before exchanging zone data. Authentication applies on a per-transaction basis for these sessions.
rules.impact: Without mutual authentication, an attacker can impersonate an authorized name server and inject unauthorized zone content. Protecting transfer sessions preserves integrity of authoritative DNS data in transit.
rules.scope: Settings in file named.conf, statements key, allow-transfer (on the primary), server and keys (on the secondary)
